generator: claude monthly run (manual, regenerated late month)
intro: Only the last week of November is left, so each deep dive fits about one week. Pick one, two or all three. Skipping is fine.

items.title: Error bars for LLM evals: is that gap real?
items.why: Most eval tables report one number per model and no uncertainty. Many claimed gains are smaller than the noise. A week with a few classic statistics tools will change how you read every benchmark table and how you design your own evals.
items.objective: Put a correct confidence interval on an eval score, compare two models with a paired test, and work out how many questions an eval needs to detect a given gap.
prerequisites: the central limit theorem at the level of an intro course

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: one model, honest error bars
tasks: Read the Anthropic post A statistical approach to model evaluations. Write the five recommendations in one line each
Read Miller, sections 1 and 2: independent questions (2.1) and clustered questions (2.2)
Simulate an eval of 500 questions in 50 clusters where questions in a cluster share difficulty. Compare the naive standard error with the clustered one
Read section 3 on variance reduction. Note why resampling answers or using next-token probabilities shrinks the error bar

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: two models, and how big an eval must be
tasks: Read Miller, section 4: unpaired versus paired analysis. Redo it in your simulation with two correlated models and see how much the paired test gains
Read section 5 on power analysis. Compute how many questions you need to detect a 2 point gap at 80 percent power
Skim Madaan et al. on seed variance in benchmarks. Note which popular benchmarks were too noisy to rank close models
Skim Dror et al. for which significance test fits which metric. Pick one recent eval table you care about and check whether its top gap would survive a paired test

primary_resource.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
primary_resource.creator: Evan Miller (Anthropic)
primary_resource.chapters: Sections 1 to 5, appendices A and B
primary_resource.note: Short and practical. Covers clustered standard errors, paired differences and power analysis, with derivations in the appendices.

resources.title: A statistical approach to model evaluations
resources.creator: Anthropic
resources.note: A plain summary of the paper as five recommendations. Read this first.

resources.title: Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks
resources.creator: Lovish Madaan, Aaditya K. Singh, Rylan Schaeffer, Andrew Poulton, Sanmi Koyejo, Pontus Stenetorp, Sharan Narang, Dieuwke Hupkes
resources.note: Measures how much benchmark scores move between training seeds.

resources.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in Natural Language Processing
resources.creator: Rotem Dror, Gili Baumer, Segev Shlomov, Roi Reichart
resources.note: ACL 2018. A guide to choosing a significance test for a given metric.

exercises: Show that for paired scores the variance of the difference is Var(A) + Var(B) - 2 Cov(A, B). Explain in two sentences why this makes paired tests stronger
Derive the sample size needed to detect a gap d with a two-sided test at level alpha and power 1 - beta, then check it against Miller's appendix B
items.deliverable: A small notebook that takes per-question scores for two models and prints a clustered confidence interval for each, a paired difference with its interval, and the eval size needed for a chosen gap.
items.definition_of_done: You can look at a benchmark table and say, with a quick calculation, whether a reported gap is likely real.
items.final_synthesis: Write one paragraph on how you would redesign an eval you use, such as adding clusters, resampling or a power check before running it.
items.light_version: Read only the Anthropic post and do the paired variance exercise on paper.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: benchmark design and contamination, or item response theory for evals. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: Survey statistics and clinical trials solved clustered samples and power long ago. LLM evals are the same problem with new names.

items.title: Philosophy of mind: what would it take for a model to be conscious?
items.why: This is the growth item for the month. Two classic essays define the hard problem. A 2023 report turns scientific theories of consciousness into concrete checks you can apply to AI systems. Together they sharpen a question interpretability keeps meeting: what does it mean to understand a mind?
items.objective: Explain the hard problem in your own words, name the main scientific theories of consciousness, and judge one current AI architecture against a list of indicator properties.
prerequisites: a rough idea of how transformers and recurrent networks work helps in week 2

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: the philosophy
tasks: Read Nagel, What Is It Like to Be a Bat? Write three sentences on why he thinks objective science may miss subjective experience
Read Chalmers, Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness: the sections on easy and hard problems and on why functional explanation seems to leave something out
Read the SEP entry Consciousness, sections 2 and 3, for the main concepts and problems. Make a one-page map of the terms

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: the science, applied to AI
tasks: Read Butlin, Long et al.: the introduction and the summaries of the five theories they use (recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing, attention schema)
Read their list of indicator properties. For a standard decoder-only transformer, mark each one as present, absent or unclear, with one line of reasons
Read SEP Consciousness, section 9, for how the specific theories are argued for and against

primary_resource.title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
primary_resource.creator: Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, Eric Elmoznino, Yoshua Bengio and 15 others
primary_resource.note: Derives indicator properties from five scientific theories and applies them to current AI systems.

resources.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
resources.creator: Thomas Nagel
resources.note: The Philosophical Review, 1974. Full text online. About 15 pages.

resources.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness
resources.creator: David J. Chalmers
resources.note: Where the easy and hard problems are named. Archive record with the full text.

resources.title: Consciousness (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
resources.creator: Robert Van Gulick
resources.note: A careful overview. Use it as a map, not a cover-to-cover read.

exercises: Write the strongest one-paragraph reply a functionalist could give to Nagel
Pick one indicator property and describe an interpretability experiment that could show whether a model has it
items.deliverable: A one-page table: the indicator properties, your verdict for a decoder-only transformer, and the experiment that would settle each unclear case.
items.definition_of_done: You can explain the hard problem and global workspace theory to a friend in five minutes, and say what evidence would change your view about model consciousness.
items.final_synthesis: Write one research question that links interpretability and consciousness science, such as whether a global broadcast mechanism can be found inside a model.
items.light_version: Read only Nagel's essay and write your three sentences.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: Dennett's Consciousness Explained, or global workspace theory in depth. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: Indicator properties turn a philosophical question into claims about mechanisms, which is the kind of thing interpretability can test.

items.title: Make a tiny explorable explanation of one idea you love
items.why: Explorable explanations let a reader drag a number and watch an idea change. Building one forces you to find the one knob that makes a concept click. It is creative coding and clear research communication in one small project.
items.objective: Build and share one single-page interactive explainer, with one slider or draggable point, for a concept you know well.
prerequisites: basic HTML and JavaScript, or willingness to learn a little
one concept you understand deeply, such as momentum, overfitting or the softmax temperature

weeks.focus: Wed 25 to Fri 27 Nov: study the masters and pick the knob
tasks: Read Bret Victor, Explorable Explanations. Note the three kinds of active reading he describes
Play with Gabriel Goh, Why Momentum Really Works, for 30 minutes. Write down which single interaction taught you the most
Read Nicky Case, How I Make Explorable Explanations. Use the three steps to choose your concept, your opening question and your closing question
Sketch your explainer on paper: one picture, one control, three sentences of text

weeks.focus: Sat 28 to Mon 30 Nov: build, test on one person, share
tasks: Work through Red Blob Games, Making of: Line drawing tutorial, up to draggable handles
Build your page with one draggable point or slider that updates a plot in real time
Watch one friend use it without help. Fix the first place they get stuck
Publish it somewhere simple, such as a GitHub Pages site, and write a two-line description

primary_resource.title: How I Make Explorable Explanations
primary_resource.creator: Nicky Case
primary_resource.note: A three-step method: start with a question, climb the ladder of abstraction, end with a question.

resources.title: Explorable Explanations
resources.creator: Bret Victor
resources.note: The essay that named the idea.

resources.title: Why Momentum Really Works
resources.creator: Gabriel Goh
resources.note: Distill. A model explorable with sliders for step size and momentum.

resources.title: Making of: Line drawing tutorial
resources.creator: Amit Patel (Red Blob Games)
resources.note: Step-by-step build of an interactive SVG diagram with draggable handles.

exercises: Write the one question your explainer answers in under 15 words
Remove every sentence that the interaction already shows
items.deliverable: A published single-page explainer with one interaction, plus a short note on what the test reader taught you.
items.definition_of_done: Someone who did not know the concept can drag the control and tell you, in their own words, what it shows.
items.final_synthesis: Write three lines on what building it taught you about the concept itself.
items.light_version: Play with Why Momentum Really Works and sketch your own explainer on paper. No code needed.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: explain one figure from your own field this way. Not scheduled automatically.

cross_domain.connection: Choosing what a reader can control is a design decision and a test of your own understanding at the same time.

plans.goal: Give a short self-introduction: nice to meet you, your name, where you are from and a polite closing.

tasks: Learn はじめまして (hajimemashite, nice to meet you) and 〇〇です (〇〇 desu, I am 〇〇). Say them out loud ten times with your own name
Learn 〇〇からきました (〇〇 kara kimashita, I came from 〇〇). Practise it with two or three place names
Read the free transcript of the JapanesePod101 self-introduction lesson and shadow the first two lines
Learn よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu, please treat me kindly, I look forward to knowing you)
Role-play meeting someone new with Claude, twice
Say all four lines in one go without notes, then answer one follow-up question from Claude

resources.title: Self-Introductions (3-Minute Japanese, lesson 1)
resources.creator: JapanesePod101
resources.note: The transcript is free to read. Audio and notes need a free account.

resources.title: Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons
resources.creator: NHK WORLD-JAPAN
resources.note: Free learner course. Optional extra listening.

plans.goal: Introduce yourself and say one thing you like, then ask how the other person is.

tasks: Review నమస్కారం (namaskāraṁ, hello). Learn నా పేరు 〇〇 (nā pēru 〇〇, my name is 〇〇) and say both out loud ten times
Learn నాకు తెలుగు అంటే ఇష్టం (nāku telugu aṇṭē iṣṭaṁ, I like Telugu). Swap in two other things you like
Read Basic Telugu, section 2.4, and say each example line out loud
Learn మీరెలా వున్నారు? (mīrelā vunnāru?, how are you?) and నేను బాగున్నాను (nēnu bāgunnānu, I am well)
Role-play a first meeting with Claude
Say the full introduction once without notes and end with ధన్యవాదాలు (dhanyavādālu, thank you)

resources.title: Basic Telugu, 2.4 Introductions and Formal Conversations
resources.creator: Afsar Mohammad and Rajiv Ranjan (MSU Libraries open textbook)
resources.note: Free open textbook. Lines in Telugu script with transliteration and English.
